video_title: Why the Next Generation of Enterprise Software Looks Nothing Like Salesforce
gist: Keith Paris, CEO of Lightfield, walks a16z partners Joe Schmidt and Alex Rampell through killing Tome (an AI presentation product at ~2 million users/month) to rebuild a CRM as a 'business world model' built on a chronological activity log rather than a predefined schema. The conversation is a detailed operating manual on cold-start distribution (free office space as 'negative pricing'), the greenfield-vs-brownfield wedge against Salesforce, a three-part pricing architecture after both pure seat and pure consumption pricing failed, and running a 40-person company with no swim lanes.

insights.claim: Tome, an AI presentation product launched around the time of ChatGPT, reached roughly 2 million users a month and about 25 million cumulative users, and its founders shut it down anyway because none of them liked the product they had built.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Raw consumer usage growth in AI-native apps can coexist with zero founder conviction; usage metrics alone are a weak signal of durable value in the LLM-wrapper category.
insights.quote: none of us like the product which is which is kind of a funny thing to say.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on AI presentation generation was missing context about the presenter, the audience and their relationship, not model reasoning ability, so waiting for better models would not have fixed the product.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A test for AI app investments: if the gap is context rather than reasoning, scaling laws will not rescue the product, and the defensible business is whoever assembles the context.
insights.quote: the model just didn't have enough context to to really understand the presenter, the audience, the relationship between the presenter and the audience and like no amount of general reasoning gets you past that.

insights.claim: The team explicitly considered shrinking headcount and waiting out the model-capability curve from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4, and rejected it because the missing ingredient was context rather than capability.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Useful diagnostic for any AI startup pitching 'the models will catch up' as the roadmap.

insights.claim: Lightfield found its B2B direction by mining Tome's existing user base for business users, discovering they were sales and marketing, then running 12 free pilots with companies of roughly 500,000 people to see what those teams actually asked for.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A repeatable pivot playbook: harvest the dead product's user base as free distribution for demand discovery rather than starting cold.

insights.claim: Sales teams pulled Lightfield away from decks into research, lead qualification and expansion analysis, and the team deliberately followed that demand rather than defending what they had built.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: The stated advantage of early-stage founders is having no priors; late-stage teams defending sunk product investment systematically miss these pivots.
insights.quote: I think what makes early stage founders good at this is that you you sort of have no priors.

insights.claim: When Lightfield asked customers for access to Salesforce, call recorders and data warehouses to do the work, it found the data was incomplete and conflicting — the call recorder frequently disagreed with the CRM — and concluded that reorganizing that reality was the more valuable and enduring business.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Identifies the actual bottleneck in the AI go-to-market tooling stack: data reconciliation, not agent execution — where the durable margin likely sits.
insights.quote: what the the call recorder often had a different view of reality than the CRM.

insights.claim: Lightfield first built a go-to-market assistant that users liked but nobody would pay for, because the company had no pricing power over data it did not own and ten competitors were selling the same layer.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Direct warning on the AI-assistant category: owning the system of record, not the workflow layer on top of it, is what creates pricing power.
insights.quote: we had all of these AES using it every day but we had no pricing power because it wasn't our data.

insights.claim: After rebuilding a CRM from first principles in the dark for four months, Lightfield could not get anyone to adopt it and bootstrapped its first ten customers by offering free space in the office it could not get rid of in exchange for using the product.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Concrete template for solving cold start in a system-of-record category where switching cost, not product quality, is the barrier.
insights.quote: I'm gonna post on X and LinkedIn. You can sit in our office space if you use our CRM.

insights.claim: The signal that the CRM was working was not satisfaction but intensity — ten startups used a slow, incomplete product daily and sent Slack complaints every two hours, in contrast with Tome's large but passive user base.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: An early-stage product-market-fit metric worth borrowing: hourly unsolicited complaint volume beats scale as an indicator of indispensability.

insights.claim: Three of Lightfield's five founding members came from Facebook, and they modeled the CRM on the Facebook timeline — building a chronological activity log of every outreach, reply, meeting, document, product usage event and payment as the canonical record, with traditional CRM fields and stages derived from it.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: The architectural bet that distinguishes this from incumbent CRMs: fields become a derived view, so schema changes can be backfilled instead of lost.

insights.claim: Lightfield tried a fully unstructured store and abandoned it because queries took too long and hit needle-in-a-haystack retrieval problems, settling on a semi-structured design that keeps large volumes of unstructured data inside the activity log for the system to infer causality from.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A practical counterexample to 'just dump everything in a vector store' architectures now common in AI enterprise products.
insights.quote: we actually tried going fully unstructured. Um and we found that uh the queries just took too long.

insights.claim: CRM consultants told Lightfield that the most consequential thing they help customers with is the data model, and that a wrong model is unrecoverable because reps will never go back in time to fill in fields — which is why Lightfield made onboarding effectively schemaless.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Names the specific incumbent failure mode that creates the opening: implementation risk, not feature gaps, is what makes traditional CRM deployments fail.
insights.quote: the biggest most consequential decision they help you with is your your data model.

insights.claim: Lightfield's organizing principle is that intelligence substitutes for schema: users connect email, a call recorder and a data warehouse, built-in enrichment runs, and relationships assemble in real time within about five minutes rather than through a configuration project.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: If schema-definition work is the real cost of enterprise software, the attack surface against incumbents is implementation time, and consulting-heavy revenue pools are at risk.
insights.quote: basically like intelligence is greater than schema.

insights.claim: Because product usage is stored as activity-log entries alongside human interactions and support tickets, a customer success user can ask open questions like which accounts to work on for expansion and have the system traverse the CRM schema and then dive into each customer's log.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Shows the concrete payoff of the log-first architecture — cross-account comparative reasoning that a conventional data lake structure makes slow or impossible.

insights.claim: Lightfield supports fully arbitrary custom objects and relationships, which let a company called Power model both a B2B pharmaceutical side and a consumer patient marketplace, scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov into a world model of every trial, and match patients to trials — reportedly helping an Alzheimer's patient find frontier treatment within days.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that arbitrary-schema systems of record can be repurposed as vertical matching engines, expanding the addressable market beyond conventional sales teams.
insights.quote: Lightfield actually helped someone with Alzheimer's find frontier treatment within days.

insights.claim: The brownfield problem in enterprise software is that incumbents hold hostages rather than customers, so a strictly better product is not sufficient to displace them — historical breaks like on-premise to cloud worked by redefining the problem, not by outperforming feature-for-feature.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for AI-native application startups: they need a redefinition of the category, not a better version of it, to unseat entrenched enterprise vendors.
insights.quote: the best companies have hostages not customers like SAP has hostages

insights.claim: Lightfield started without a thesis for entering brownfield accounts, deliberately targeted new companies via LinkedIn prospecting and cold emails to YC startups, and used six months of watching those customers scale to discover the real wedge.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Argues that the ICP for a system-of-record startup should be chosen for iteration speed and observability, not for immediate revenue.

insights.claim: Serving early-stage startups is unusually valuable right now because companies move from pre-seed to seed to A to B faster than ever, so Lightfield has customers that joined with zero reps and now have about 100 reps — compressing years of enterprise learning into months.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A reason to re-rate startup-focused SaaS: faster customer graduation converts a low-ACV base into enterprise ACV inside a normal fund cycle.

insights.claim: Lightfield's contrarian bet is that the brownfield wedge is helping leaders understand and steer their company, not 'do the work' automation like lead scoring and outbound email, which is what every AI CRM billboard in Silicon Valley has advertised and which Salesforce can replicate.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: If correct, AI-SDR and outbound-automation startups are competing in the layer incumbents can most easily absorb, while understanding/forecasting is the defensible ground.

insights.claim: Lightfield gives the product away free to everyone in the company on sales-led plans, deliberately creating company-wide network effects across engineering, support and finance so that an incoming Salesforce-trained VP of sales is pressured by colleagues rather than able to rip and replace.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A concrete defense against the well-known pattern where a newly hired executive reverts the stack to the incumbent they were trained on.
insights.quote: it'll create sort of real company network effects that make it harder to rip and replace us.

insights.claim: Lightfield chose pragmatism over AI purism — keeping dashboards, spreadsheet views and tables because the CEO himself runs sales meetings from the spreadsheet view — while offering chat, MCP and CLI access for frontier users.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Suggests deterministic dashboards remain table stakes in enterprise software; chat-only AI-native products are likely under-serving the buyer.
insights.quote: if we really want to be like a real enterprise CRM, we can't be religious about the way people work.

insights.claim: Lightfield replaced the classic sales sequence builder — arrows, conditions and variables — with a chat interaction where an agent writes a recipe that reads from the world model, and sales leaders who initially distrusted it came around once they had less to learn.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A live example of the visual-workflow-builder category being collapsed into natural language, which threatens marketing-automation tooling built on that UI paradigm.

themes.theme: Pricing after seat and credit failures

insights.claim: Lightfield started with pure seat pricing to match the Salesforce and HubSpot model, and it failed on unit economics because the heaviest users consumed roughly 10,000 times more than the lightest ones.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Quantifies why per-seat pricing breaks for inference-heavy software — a margin risk for any incumbent SaaS vendor bolting AI onto existing seat contracts.
insights.quote: the head just the head was using 10,000x more than the tail.

insights.claim: Pure consumption pricing, with everything denominated in credits, froze customer behavior entirely — signups stopped touching the product — in what the CEO called the worst three weeks of the company's life.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that metered pricing suppresses adoption in daily-use software, cutting against the current enthusiasm for all-consumption AI pricing.
insights.quote: then we found that nobody touched anything.

insights.claim: Lightfield segments its work into four buckets — everyday CRM capture and record updates, pipeline generation, workflow automation, and intelligence/forecasting — and charges a fixed platform fee plus seats for the first while metering the rest, because customers refuse budget uncertainty on core CRM.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A transferable hybrid pricing template for AI software: fix the price of the system of record, meter the work and the alpha.
insights.quote: I don't want to think about the like error bounds of my core CRM when I look at my budget

insights.claim: Lightfield rejected outcome-based pricing for sales software because its outcomes depend on the customer's own product-market fit — outbound for OpenAI would be trivially effective while outbound for a seed-stage startup with no website would not — so it charges for work instead.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Explains why outcome pricing generalizes to support (a measurable cost center) but not to revenue-generating categories where the vendor cannot control the input quality.
insights.quote: we can't quite charge for the outcome in the space uh for now.

insights.claim: Seed-stage founders routinely told Lightfield they could build the same thing over four weekends, and the ones who tried came back reporting hallucinations and bad outbound emails.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Field evidence that the 'SaaS is dead, vibe-code it yourself' thesis is overstated at the system-of-record layer, at least today.

insights.claim: Larger companies do not say they will build their own system of record — they say they will build their own company brain — and they return after discovering that modeling customers is the hardest part of building a business world model.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Identifies where internal AI platform projects fail, and therefore what a vendor must own to stay non-replicable: the customer entity model.
insights.quote: I'm going to build my own company brain

insights.claim: Customers who used Lightfield as the system of record and built their own harness on top via MCP or CLI generally reverted within a few weeks because Lightfield's harness delivered better entity recognition, better precision and recall, and more speed.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Suggests retrieval quality — not data storage — is the real moat for AI systems of record, and that openness is a safe strategy when the harness is genuinely better.
insights.quote: after a few weeks, they almost always realize, wait a minute, your harness was actually doing quite a bit.

insights.claim: Lightfield eliminated functional swim lanes after concluding that Tome's siloed product, marketing and CS leaders — 'playing house' — slowed the company to a crawl and made pivoting impossible because the appendages were not talking to the brain.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Ties org structure directly to pivot optionality, a specific diligence question for AI-era startups that may need to re-found themselves.
insights.quote: we had a lot of people playing house

insights.claim: Lightfield runs 40 people with one company-wide daily standup, a stack-ranked list of the most important problems spanning delivery, engineering and CS, continuous daily replanning, and whoever is free picking up the next problem — with engineers, designers and CSMs all running projects.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A concrete operating model for AI-era companies; it works only because AI tooling lets anyone ramp on customers, design systems and task creation.
insights.quote: we have 40 people at the company. Everyone shows up to the same standup every morning.

insights.claim: Coherence in a generalist, no-swim-lane organization is maintained by a weekly go-to-market roadmap edit that rejects customer requests that do not fit the mission, plus an asymmetric quality gate: a very low bar to start a project and a high bar to ship it, enforced through company-wide bug bashes learned at Instagram.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: The missing control system for 'everyone can build anything' organizations — the constraint moves from build capacity to shipping standards and editing.
insights.quote: the bar to start a project is very low at lightfield but the bar to ship the project is pretty high

insights.claim: The CEO's biggest fear is shipping speed, citing teardown reports of companies migrating from startup CRMs back to Salesforce — including 11 Labs, which moved after waiting roughly four months for dashboards it never got.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Names the specific churn mechanism for AI-native system-of-record startups: feature latency on mundane requests, not AI quality, sends customers back to incumbents.
insights.quote: they couldn't get that company to build dashboards fast enough

insights.claim: Lightfield prioritizes by projected three-year expansion value of an account rather than average customer need, on the view that in a red-ocean CRM market the initial land will be small and the company must be an expansion business — so it builds for its fastest-growing customers.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A prioritization rule for competitive categories where land economics are structurally unattractive and all the value sits in net revenue retention.
insights.quote: as a CRM company in a red ocean space we have to be an expansion company

insights.claim: A CRM is described as harder to move off of than a bank, which makes vertical referenceability — proof that companies that look like you already made the switch — the dominant factor in system-of-record purchasing even though the underlying customer data is identical across industries.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Explains why go-to-market for systems of record is logo-sequencing by vertical rather than feature marketing, and why breaking into each new vertical has a fixed cost.
insights.quote: your your CRM is maybe harder to move off of than your bank.

insights.claim: Lightfield wins health tech deals easily today because it invested early in security — signing BAAs and running penetration testing for years — and because its context engineering handles complex deals with around 50 stakeholders.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Early compliance spend acts as a vertical moat; startups that defer it lose the regulated segments where reference networks compound fastest.

insights.claim: AI is arguably overhyped inside Silicon Valley and massively underhyped everywhere else, partly because non-Valley buyers tried ChatGPT once in November 2022, saw it hallucinate, and have not revisited it since.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Frames the adoption gap as the largest remaining commercial opportunity, and implies distribution — not model capability — is the binding constraint on AI revenue outside tech.
insights.quote: AI is almost overhyped in Silicon Valley. I don't think it is but and it's like massively underhyped outside of this little region of the world.

insights.claim: System-of-record companies take most of their revenue scale from outside the Bay Area, so Lightfield treats Silicon Valley customers — including ones that raised $200 million with only three go-to-market people — as efficient marketing capture for reference logos rather than efficient revenue capture.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Reframes how to read a startup's Valley-heavy customer list: as vertical entry credentials, not as the addressable revenue base.
insights.quote: I just see the focus on Silicon Valley not as a not as efficient revenue capture, but actually just like efficient marketing capture

themes.theme: Forecasting as the next product surface

insights.claim: Lightfield's least-discovered and most valuable bucket is intelligence and forecasting — deploying frontier models against a company's own modeled reality for scenario planning — and the CEO says he changed his own sales process after letting GPT-6 run on Lightfield for a couple of hours on a weekend.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: If scenario planning becomes the willingness-to-pay center of gravity, value shifts from workflow software toward whoever holds the complete, machine-readable business model.

insights.claim: One Lightfield customer selling into enterprise discovered through the system that it needed a mid-market product and built an entirely new product line as a result, illustrating strategy decisions previously requiring analysts, ops teams and SQL being made in an afternoon.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Concrete proof point for the 'company crystal ball' thesis and for pricing intelligence separately from CRM seats.

insights.claim: The advice for founders mid-pivot is that virtually all surrounding noise — office culture nostalgia, food quality, option repricing — is irrelevant, and the only tasks are finding real pain, building something that solves it and staying maniacally focused on customers.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A filter for evaluating whether a pivoting portfolio company is managing its team's anxiety or actually relocating to real demand.
insights.quote: almost none of the noise around you matters when you're in a pivot.

insights.claim: The shift from tightly predefined relational schemas — where a column like name was declared varchar(25) to save space — to schemaless AI systems is framed as the same transition as cars losing physical controls, where removing knobs and switches makes the tool intuitive enough for anyone rather than only for trained specialists.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Frames the competitive threat to expertise-gated enterprise tools like Bloomberg terminals and legacy CRMs: their configurability was a constraint artifact, not a feature.

insights.claim: Deterministic dashboards remain unbeaten despite the shift to natural language, because users still want to look at the same dashboard every morning with their coffee.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Tempers the thesis that conversational interfaces replace BI; the recurring-glance use case is a durable product requirement and likely a durable category.
insights.quote: we haven't won the war on uh you know deterministic dashboards.
